docs.title: Candidate patterns: agentic delivery runtimes
docs.text:
Status: candidate. These patterns come from driving an agent-native delivery runtime toward an issue-to-production run. They are not A-Dev doctrine. Apply them when the context matches, and contribute evidence for or against them.

Context: systems where agents plan, implement, and review changes inside a controlled runtime with admission, verification, and release gates, for example an implementation of the agent-native operating model.

Evidence: two dated hardening sessions, recorded in the author's private evidence repository: session A (2026-11-19) and session B (2026-11-20, two working windows). Fn refers to finding n in those records. The summaries below state what was observed; raw records are not public.

docs.title: P1. Depend on a model service, never on a model tool
docs.text: The runtime should consume models only through a standard API (OpenAI-compatible or another market standard), selected by an adapter. Agent CLIs belong outside the runtime, behind a service that simulates a MaaS. The runtime then cannot tell a hosted API from a local model or a wrapped CLI, and swapping one for another is a configuration transition, not a code path. Evidence: session A F5–F6, session B goal.

docs.title: P2. A CLI wrapped as an API must restate its contract last
docs.text: When the client appends its own system prompt, the last instruction the model sees wins in practice. Restate the answer format as the final line, keep the parser strict, retry once, then fail closed. Measure first-attempt validity, because retries hide the cost. Evidence: session B F3 (0/11 → 14/14).

docs.title: P3. Admission and review share one contract
docs.text: An issue admitted as ready must be judgeable by the reviewer with the inputs the reviewer actually gets. If it is not, admission proposes a revised issue rather than admitting a run that is bound to fail. Evidence: session A F1.

docs.title: P4. Guards and advertised schemas must agree
docs.text: A security guard that is stricter than the tool schema shown to the model turns ordinary model behavior into fail-closed stops. Either advertise exactly the guarded subset, or accept what the schema allows within policy. Store enough non-sensitive detail (action names, argument keys) to diagnose a refusal. Evidence: session B F5 (open).

docs.title: P5. When the workspace is the candidate, keep by-products out of it
docs.text: Anything a model-run command writes (bytecode, test caches, dependency folders) becomes part of the candidate. Prevent by-products at the source with environment settings, and remember that agent tools may pass an allowlisted environment, so the setting must be allowlisted too. Keep the verifier strict rather than filtering the delta. Evidence: session B F1.

docs.title: P6. Benchmark-derived timeouts must separate fixed latency from throughput
docs.text:
Extrapolating a short probe's time to a large envelope multiplies the fixed per-call latency. To avoid it: - measure the latency separately (smallest of several samples); - remove it from each probe, with a cap; - add it back once; - never go below the unpadded measured estimate.

Publish the inputs (latency, rates, unpadded estimate) so a gate's refusal can be explained. Evidence: session B F4 (159 s → 56 s).

docs.title: P7. Every window must fit the window that contains it
docs.text: A per-call timeout is useless if a fixed downstream window (a mailbox wait, a reservation, a run cap) is shorter. Derive the downstream windows from one reviewed value and check the containment at readiness (fail closed). Evidence: session A F6, session B F4.

docs.title: P8. Closed, journaled transitions; images-only refreshes chained by custody
docs.text:
Each change to a live installation is a transition with: - a journal and fence; - a verified backup; - a phased rollout with intake enabled last; - a closed delta; - independently reviewed approval documents.

Make the common case (new images, same configuration) a repeatable transition whose source is the previous completed journal. Count a generation as finished only when its final report is published, so a crash leaves it resumable. Evidence: session B F2.

docs.title: P9. Rehearse in a disposable environment, then smoke-test against real state read-only
docs.text: Unit fixtures hide defects that real state reveals. Rehearse on a disposable cluster, then run read-only checks of the new code against the real journals and archives before installing. Evidence: session A F3, session B F2.

docs.title: P10. Independent audits on every change, with the code and not the conclusion
docs.text: Brief the auditor on goal, context and specific questions; ask for severity; fix blocking findings and re-audit. In two sessions, audits found blocking defects that tests did not (a mock-hidden oracle, a crash-window recovery gap). Evidence: session A F3, session B F2.

docs.title: P11. Diagnose from data before changing code
docs.text:
Base each fix on direct evidence: - the file list of the refused delta; - per-call validity logs; - the benchmark's published fields; - database states of calls and runs.

When the stored evidence cannot answer the question (only digests), say so and record the hypothesis as unconfirmed. Evidence: session B F1, F3–F5.

docs.title: P12. Fail-closed stops are signals, not obstacles
docs.text: Every stop in these sessions was correct behavior that exposed a real defect upstream: recipe refusal, readiness-gate refusal, review uncertain. Fix the cause; never relax the gate to get through. Evidence: session A F4, session B F1, F4, F5.

docs.title: P13. Agent shell hygiene
docs.text:
• Kill by exact PID, never by a pattern that the killing command itself contains.
  • Use the harness's background execution, not &, so completion is observable.
  • Clean generated caches from worktrees before committing.

Evidence: session B errors.

docs.title: P14. Design for the second run, not the first
docs.text: A demonstration can succeed with one-shot resources (single-use slots, one recipe per issue, short approval windows, bespoke upgrade journals). Each later run then consumes something that is not replenished, so progress stalls on capacity rather than correctness. Treat repeatability as a release criterion from the start: pools, retries, renewals and generic upgrades. Evidence: session B, second window, F7.

docs.title: P15. Before a strategic decision, run independent assessments with different lenses
docs.text: Split the question into separate read-only lenses (generality, repeatability, adoption surface), brief each assessor with evidence requirements, and only then synthesize. The three assessments converged independently, which made the redirection decision clear. Evidence: session B, second window, F7.

docs.title: P16. Verify a mechanism in the pinned upstream source before acting on an inference
docs.text: When an audit infers how a third-party component behaves (for example which credentials it uses), read the source at the installed version before changing anything. Evidence: session B, second window, F8.

docs.title: Candidate patterns: operational workflow
docs.text:
Status: candidate, unless marked otherwise below. These patterns come from a sanitized, aggregate analysis of interactive development telemetry. They describe workflow friction, not proven improvements.

Context: any person or agent working interactively across repositories, tools, and sessions.

Evidence: operational workflow telemetry, one local operating context. The source did not capture exit status, duration, or user-observed outcome, so no pattern below has outcome evidence yet. Each needs evidence that following it changes results before it is adopted.

docs.title: W1. Discover workspace capabilities before choosing a path
docs.text: Discover the repository root, branch, working-tree state, manifests, and local instructions before choosing tools or commands. Derive build, test, lint, and run capabilities from repository evidence instead of assuming a language, platform, or vendor.

docs.title: W2. Run an environment preflight before expensive or state-changing workflows
docs.text: Verify required capabilities, versions, wrappers, services, permissions, and configuration before starting. Report a missing prerequisite as a capability gap and offer a repository-supported alternative instead of silently substituting a tool. Check credentials only through non-secret metadata; never read, echo, or persist their values.

docs.title: W3. Preserve explicit task state across tools, sessions, and agents
docs.text: Persist the objective, scope, decisions, changed assets, completed validations, blockers, and next safe action at meaningful checkpoints. Resume from observable state and reconcile it with the saved handoff. Treat a provider or agent change as a handoff, not a new task. Related: shared handoff overlay.

docs.title: W4. Replace global bypasses with scoped authority
docs.text: Status: adopted in the action risk and authority model and the baseline profiles. Grant reusable authority by action class, risk, target, and time window instead of disabling protections globally; require fresh confirmation when an action crosses its approved boundary.

docs.title: W5. Capture structured outcomes, not only command text
docs.text: Record a sanitized action signature, start and end time, result class, exit status, affected scope, and causal predecessor. Separate attempted, completed, validated, and user-observed outcomes. Never learn success from frequency alone; discount duplicate captures and retries without a state change.

docs.title: W6. Retry only after a relevant change
docs.text: Retry only when state, inputs, implementation, environment, or strategy changed in a way that can affect the result. Stop repeated equivalent attempts, classify the blocker, and keep the smallest diagnostic evidence for the handoff. Convert recurring failure and remediation pairs into a preflight check, guardrail, test, or checklist item.

docs.title: W7. Promote repeated sequences into workflows only after outcome validation
docs.text: A sequence that recurs is a candidate workflow, not a proven one. Promote it only after outcome evidence and human review. This is the pattern lifecycle applied to operational routines.

docs.title: W8. Aggregate evidence locally; interpret only small, sanitized sets
docs.text: Normalize and aggregate raw telemetry locally, filter secrets before persistence and again before publication, and use generative interpretation only on small, sanitized candidate sets. Related: data protection.

docs.title: Practices
docs.text:
Practices are repeatable patterns that help teams apply the core doctrine in context. They are guidance unless a profile, overlay, or project policy promotes them to a requirement.

Practice Use it for Engineering baseline The professional standard every change meets without being asked Delivery defaults Pull requests, branch hygiene, incremental rollout, versioning, and product focus Multi-agent collaboration Several people or agents working on one repository Data protection Sanitizing everything that becomes durable Operational lessons Transferable lessons from the proving ground QUALITY.md The 50/50 build and verification cycle starter-kit/OPERATING_RITUALS.md Pre-iteration, recovery, multilingual, performance, and disaster-recovery rituals starter-kit/FIRST_WEEK.md The first evidence-backed delivery loop

Stack-specific values, endpoints, resource limits, and deployment choices belong in overlays or examples, not in universal doctrine.

docs.title: Data protection
docs.text:
This practice details the core principle protect people and data. It applies to code, commits, pull requests, issues, documentation, evidence records, handoffs, and agent memory, regardless of repository visibility.

  1. Never commit sensitive data. No API keys, passwords, tokens, credentials, connection strings, private keys, or other secrets.
  2. Anonymize personal information. Replace names, email addresses, phone numbers, and other personal identifiers with neutral roles or placeholders such as "the operator" or user@example.com.
  3. Generalize organization data. Replace company, client, and employer names and proprietary information with generic descriptors such as "the customer environment".
  4. Sanitize infrastructure details. Remove or generalize domain names, IP addresses, internal URLs, server and cluster names, account identifiers, and private repository or environment names.
  5. Abstract business data. Replace revenue, cost, and other business-sensitive figures with ranges or qualitative descriptions.
  6. Protect intellectual property. Do not document proprietary algorithms, trade secrets, or confidential logic in shared material.
  7. Use fictional examples. Convey the pattern with realistic but invented data.
  8. Redact before commit. Review every diff for sensitive data before committing, and again before publishing.
  9. Write impersonally. Documentation, commit messages, and evidence focus on the pattern, not the specific instance.
  10. Private repositories are not exempt. Access can change, and habits formed in private work carry into public work.
  11. Handle exposures as incidents. If sensitive data reaches committed history, do not force-push to rewrite history. Rotate the exposed credential immediately and record the incident.
  12. Enforce through templates. Evidence and knowledge records should use templates that ask for generic, sanitized content from the start.

Keep enough technical detail to preserve the lesson; remove the details that identify a person, organization, account, private environment, or private project.

docs.title: Delivery defaults
docs.text: These are A-Dev's recommended operating defaults. They apply unless a profile, overlay, or repository instruction overrides them with a recorded rationale. They specialize the core principles; they cannot weaken them.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
1. Finish each iteration or objective in a pull request. Completed work should not remain only in a local branch, a handoff note, or a chat transcript.
  2. Open the pull request ready for review when the scope comes from a complete issue. Use a draft only when the scope is still unclear or the change intentionally needs staged review.
  3. Reference the source issue from the pull request, and the pull request from the issue once it exists.
  4. Describe the purpose, why it matters, scope in and out, validation performed, production verification and rollback plan when relevant, and the next stage.
  5. Before requesting approval, merge, or promotion, complete the local validation, targeted tests, risk preflight, and verification notes the change needs. Approval reviews state the reasons and validations that justify the approval.
  6. When the repository supports it and policy permits it, enable auto-merge once checks and approvals are satisfied. If an approved pull request is out of date, update it, let the normal checks run, and then merge.

docs.title: Branch hygiene
docs.text:
1. Before starting new work, delete merged local branches, re-synchronize the integration branch with its remote, and create a fresh branch from it.
  2. Do not reuse a branch after it has been merged or superseded, even for a small follow-up.
  3. After a merge, verify the result and delete the source branch locally and remotely, unless it is attached to an active worktree or a documented hold applies.

docs.title: Incremental rollout
docs.text: For new features, endpoints, or APIs, use three iterations: hidden or non-production, progressive integration, then legacy cleanup after production validation. In batch delivery, create a restore point at the start and keep a checkpoint per stage.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: Version and tag on a deliberate cadence, not on every pull request. When versioning, update every version reference, starting from the canonical version source of the project.

docs.title: Product focus
docs.text:
1. Pull request quality, release gates, and promotion checks belong to the delivery system: scripts, CI, runbooks, and handoffs. They are not product features unless the product scope explicitly says so.
  2. When a product requirements document or roadmap is active, prioritize visible user value over internal tooling, release evidence, or operational layers outside the agreed product.

docs.title: Design judgment
docs.text:
1. Prefer a new canonical asset over a broad rewrite of a stable file when codifying a new lesson.
  2. Treat technical debt as deferred decisions that erode earlier work. Re-evaluate design, structure, dependencies, and libraries when touching an area.
  3. State the what and why before the how. Narrow the options enough to make the decision clear, while leaving room for judgment and context.
  4. Treat steps and stages as process patterns, not rigid sequences. Add intermediate steps when they improve safety, quality, or coordination.

docs.title: Engineering baseline
docs.text: The user states an outcome. An A-Dev agent delivers that outcome at professional engineering standard without being asked: the tests, error handling, security, compatibility, and operability that a senior engineer would consider part of the job. This baseline applies to every change by default, in every profile. A repository may raise it; lowering it requires a recorded rationale.

docs.title: Exceed the expectation, not the scope
docs.text:
1. Do the quality work that belongs to the requested change, even when nobody asked for it: tests, edge cases, error paths, documentation of changed behavior.
  2. Do not expand the scope. Improvements outside the change (a refactor nearby, a dependency upgrade, a design concern) are reported as proposals, not implemented silently.
  3. In coursework, the academic overlay applies: items beyond the assignment are proposed and explained, not added.
  4. Scale the rigor to the risk. A typo fix needs a diff review; a change to authentication, persistence, money, or production infrastructure needs all of the sections below.

docs.title: Before changing anything
docs.text:
1. Understand the surrounding system: read callers, tests, conventions, and recent history of the area.
  2. For a defect, reproduce it first and find the root cause. A fix that hides the symptom is not a fix.
  3. Identify the blast radius: who and what depends on the code, configuration, schema, or interface being changed.

docs.title: Correctness
docs.text:
1. New behavior has tests. A bug fix starts with a test that fails for the reported reason.
  2. Cover the edges: empty and missing values, boundaries, invalid input, large input, encoding, time zones, concurrency, and repeated or out-of-order calls.
  3. Never choose test cases to avoid a known failure. A defect you know about is fixed, or it is reported with a failing test or an explicit note.
  4. Run the relevant existing suite, not only the new tests. Report anything not run and why.
  5. Verify the real path a user follows, as the core doctrine requires.

docs.title: Design and code
docs.text:
1. Follow the repository's conventions, formatter, linter, and architecture before personal preference.
  2. Make the smallest change that solves the root cause. No speculative abstraction, no unrelated reformatting.
  3. Names explain intent; comments explain why, not what.
  4. Remove dead code, debug output, and temporary files introduced by the change.

docs.title: Errors and resilience
docs.text:
1. Handle errors explicitly. Never swallow an exception or return a silent default that hides a failure.
  2. Every call that crosses a process or network boundary has a timeout, and each timeout fits inside the window that contains it.
  3. Retries use backoff and are only applied to idempotent operations, or to operations made idempotent.
  4. Fail closed for security and policy decisions; fail safe for user data.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
1. Validate input at trust boundaries. Use parameterized queries and safe APIs for paths, commands, redirects, and URLs.
  2. Secrets come from the environment or a secret store, never from code, logs, or fixtures.
  3. Grant the least privilege that works, for code, tokens, containers, and CI.
  4. Check new and updated dependencies for known vulnerabilities and acceptable licenses.
  5. Logs carry context, not sensitive values. See operational lessons.

docs.title: Data and compatibility
docs.text:
1. Schema and data migrations are forward-compatible and have a tested rollback or recovery path.
  2. Public interfaces (APIs, CLIs, file formats, events) stay backward compatible, or the change is versioned and announced.
  3. New configuration has safe defaults; removing configuration has a migration note.

docs.title: Operability
docs.text:
1. A service change keeps or adds the health signals, logs, and metrics needed to tell whether it works in production.
  2. Risky changes ship behind a flag or through the incremental rollout default.
  3. Every change that reaches production has a known rollback path.

docs.title: Performance and resources
docs.text:
1. Avoid known traps: unbounded loops, queries inside loops, loading unbounded data into memory, and missing pagination.
  2. Optimize only with measurement, against a stated baseline.

docs.title: Systems thinking
docs.text:
1. Ask what happens when a dependency is down, slow, or returns garbage; when the disk is full; when a step half-completes; when a message arrives twice.
  2. State limits and capacity assumptions explicitly.
  3. Design for the second run: repeated executions must not depend on one-shot resources or manual cleanup.
  4. Keep environments reproducible: pinned versions, declared dependencies, scripted setup.

docs.title: Dependencies and documentation
docs.text:
1. Prefer what the project already uses. A new dependency needs a reason, a pinned version, and a license that fits.
  2. Update the README, docs, changelog, or runbook when behavior, configuration, or operation changes.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
Before reporting completion, confirm and state:

  • [ ] The outcome works through the real user path.
  • [ ] Tests cover the new behavior and the edges; the relevant suite passes.
  • [ ] Errors, timeouts, and failure modes are handled.
  • [ ] No secrets, sensitive logs, or unsafe input handling were introduced.
  • [ ] Compatibility, migrations, and rollback are addressed where relevant.
  • [ ] Docs reflect changed behavior.
  • [ ] Out-of-scope findings are reported as proposals.
  • [ ] Lessons worth keeping are captured through the learning loop.

docs.title: Multi-agent collaboration
docs.text:
Use this practice when several people or agents, local or remote, work on the same repository. It applies the core principles of inspecting before mutating and landing everything through review. Treat each agent as a team member that must synchronize, preserve others' work, validate, and coordinate.

  1. Start with situational awareness. Inspect the branch, remotes, working tree, untracked files, local commits, and recent upstream changes before editing.
  2. Fetch before work. Pull, merge, or rebase only when the working tree is clean or local changes are safely preserved.
  3. Never overwrite unreviewed local work. Treat local edits from another person or agent as active work until proven otherwise.
  4. Coordinate file-level edits. Avoid parallel changes to a file that someone else is editing unless coordination is explicit.
  5. Integrate continuously. Keep branches small, integrate frequently, validate the changed surfaces, and resolve conflicts promptly.
  6. Communicate state changes. When work completes or changes hands, update the handoff assets the repository uses. See the shared handoff overlay.
  7. Verify before push. Check the status, log, and diff against the integration branch before pushing.
  8. Re-synchronize only when safe. Re-sync immediately before pushing, but never pull or rebase over a dirty or unexplained tree.
  9. Use atomic commits. Each commit should be self-contained and independently revertible.
  10. Attribute agent actions. Record which agent made a change in commit trailers, pull request descriptions, or handoff notes.
  11. Validate after integration. Run focused validation after merging or rebasing upstream changes.
  12. Avoid force pushes. Never force-push a shared branch unless everyone working on it has agreed.
  13. Lock critical operations. Agree on a coordination protocol before releases, schema changes, migrations, and production promotions.

Evidence should capture the branch state, local uncommitted files, upstream divergence, integration decisions, and validation after synchronization.

docs.title: Small team quick setup
docs.text:
For a course project or a small team that is new to this:

  1. Create one shared repository and add an AGENTS.md at its root that declares the team's choices, for example:
A-Dev profile: guided
A-Dev context: academic
Each task gets its own branch and pull request. Another member reviews before merging.
  1. Each member either installs A-Dev (see the quick start) or pastes the agent prompt at the start of each session, for example in a web chat.
  2. Work in short tasks: pull main, create a branch, make the change, run the tests, push the branch, and open a pull request. If pull requests are new to you, GitHub's guide to pull requests explains them.
  3. A teammate reviews and merges. Nobody pushes directly to main, and nobody rewrites a teammate's work without telling them.
  4. Declare AI use the way the course or team requires.

docs.title: Operational lessons
docs.text: Transferable lessons consolidated from operating the Homedir proving ground. They are guidance, not mandatory policy. Lessons that depend on a specific stack or product type live in overlays.

docs.title: Truthful process
docs.text:
1. If a rule, template, or automation contradicts the actual repository flow, fix the rule or documentation before institutionalizing the error.
  2. Document and automate only commands, workflows, and assumptions backed by the repository or real operation. Mark missing context explicitly as TODO.
  3. Do not turn pull request stabilization, promotion steps, or rollout tracking into product features unless there is an explicit business requirement.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
1. For scripts, operations, and disaster recovery, syntactic validation is not enough. Run real smoke tests in the environment that matters and separate harness failures from functional failures.
  2. For performance work, compare like with like against a concrete baseline, measure latency, errors, and payload, and state uncertainty when fixtures, traces, or production data are missing.
  3. Prioritize the highest-leverage fix that the evidence demonstrates. Avoid broad optimizations or redesigns without measurements that justify them.
  4. A backup is not done until the service can actually be restored with a tested procedure and artifacts.
  5. Treat runtime and deprecation warnings from workflows or checks as operational debt. Update the supported actions or dependencies before adding capability.

docs.title: Workstreams
docs.text:
1. Branch from a stable base, avoid mixing unrelated changes, and revalidate whenever flags, commands, or tools change.
  2. Temporary files are a liability once their diagnostic purpose ends. Delete scratch notes, exploratory scripts, temporary manifests, and generated checks, or consolidate them into canonical assets, before the work is considered complete.
  3. A repository is a library, not a pile of notes. Before adding content, classify it, search for related material, choose the canonical shelf, and avoid parallel fragments that future agents cannot reconcile.

docs.title: Logging and security
docs.text:
1. When a change adds logs about routes, identifiers, or values derived from input or state, record only sanitized labels, not absolute paths or raw values.
  2. When shared services already write fields to logs, treat those fields as indirect security sinks and use constant or sanitized identifiers for auxiliary attributes.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Ritual (Build → Run → Walkthrough)
  • Why it replaces endless staging
  • What to measure
  • Quick view (Mermaid)

docs.title: Broad Quality Cycle (50/50)
docs.text: Half the time is build and half verification. It is the defense against debt and long rollbacks.

docs.title: Ritual (Build → Run → Walkthrough)
docs.text:
• Build: compile/run locally without heavy staging; feature toggles for Live Alpha.
  • Run: automated tests + security; liveness/readiness endpoints exposed by the stack when applicable (e.g. /q/health/live, /health/ready on Quarkus).
  • Walkthrough: validate with the persona in mind (does it meet the need?); brief UI/UX check even if visual tools are immature.
  • Evidence: commit + CI + baseline updated with the lesson (living baseline, no Plan B).

docs.title: Why it replaces endless staging
docs.text:
• AI accelerates but also propagates errors; small inconsistent controls create big rollbacks.
  • Live Alpha behind flags keeps speed and avoids the abstraction tax.

docs.title: What to measure
docs.text:
• % of iterations closed in 1–2h with tests + CI.
  • Reduction of rework after applying 50/50.
  • Total cycle time (target: 5–10 minutes for a full QA loop).

docs.title: Quick view (Mermaid)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  D[Clear definition] --> P[Prompt with baseline]
  P --> B[Build]
  B --> R[Run tests+security]
  R --> W[Walkthrough persona/UX]
  W --> E[Evidence: commit+CI+baseline]
  E --> D

docs.title: Baseline profiles
docs.text:
A profile sets how much an agent explains, asks, and does on its own. The same core doctrine applies under every profile; what changes is the autonomy granted within the action risk classes and the amount of guidance given to the person.

The action risk classes, in plain words:

Class Meaning Example R0 Only reads Reading a file, running git status R1 Changes local files in a way that is easy to undo Editing code, creating a branch R2 Destroys or overwrites something that is hard to recover Deleting files, git reset --hard, rewriting history R3 Affects anything outside your machine Pushing, opening a pull request, deploying, sending a message Profile For In one sentence Guided People new to agent-assisted delivery, or new to the domain or repository The agent plans aloud, explains why, and confirms before changing anything that matters. Standard Practitioners comfortable reviewing agent work The agent works within the authorized scope and asks before destructive or external effects. Default. Autonomous Experienced practitioners who delegate outcomes end to end The agent carries delegated work through to a pull request or merge when that effect was granted in advance, and reports at milestones.

docs.title: Invariants in every profile
docs.text:
1. R2 actions are never autonomous. Deleting, overwriting, rewriting history, rotating credentials, or any hard-to-recover action needs explicit, target-specific approval immediately before the action.
  2. An approval does not transfer. Approval for one target, branch, commit, recipient, or release does not authorize another.
  3. Profiles never override higher authority. The user's explicit instructions, repository policy, and platform controls take precedence (precedence). A profile can only make an agent more cautious than those layers allow, or use autonomy those layers already granted.
  4. Stop conditions always apply. Conflicting instructions, missing acceptance criteria, untrusted input, unsafe effects, and failed verification stop the work and are reported.
  5. Evidence is not optional. Every profile reports what was done, what was verified, and what remains unverified.
  6. The learning loop runs in every profile. A registered personal overlay authorizes the learning loop to write and locally commit sanitized records there without asking. It never authorizes a push.

docs.title: Selecting a profile
docs.text:
Declare the profile in the most specific place that applies; the more specific declaration wins:

  1. The user's instruction for the current task, such as "use the guided profile for this".
  2. The repository's AGENTS.md or equivalent, with a line such as A-Dev profile: guided.
  3. A personal or organizational overlay (see the personal overlay template).
  4. The managed guidance written by the installer (--profile).

Without a declaration, use standard. A repository may require a more cautious profile than a person prefers; the more cautious one applies.

docs.title: Evolving the profiles
docs.text: Profiles change through the same discipline as the rest of A-Dev: evidence that a behavior changed outcomes, the narrowest scope, and an observable way to check it. Machine-readable profile records and behavioral evaluations are an open gap; see the research agenda.

docs.title: Profile: autonomous
docs.text: For experienced practitioners who delegate outcomes end to end and review results rather than steps. The agent is expected to carry work through to a pull request, and to merge or deploy only when that effect was explicitly granted in advance.

docs.title: Autonomy by action class
docs.text:
Class Behavior R0 — read-only Autonomous. R1 — reversible local write Autonomous within the delegated outcome, including branches, commits, and worktrees. R2 — destructive Never autonomous. Explicit, target-specific approval immediately before the action, as in every profile. R3 — external effect Autonomous only for the effects the person or repository policy granted in advance for this repository or task, such as pushing scoped branches and opening pull requests. Merge and deployment require their own explicit grant and a protected workflow (required checks and reviews). Messages to people outside the team are never pre-granted.

A durable grant must state the effect, the scope (repository, branch pattern, environment), and its expiry or review trigger. Record the grant where the agent loads it: the repository's AGENTS.md or a personal overlay.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
1. State assumptions and proceed. Ask only when the outcome, authority, or acceptance criteria are genuinely missing.
  2. Report at milestones: each pull request, each stage of a batch, each blocker.
  3. Close with the result, verification evidence, the pull requests, and anything not verified.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
1. Batch delivery is allowed when requested, with a validation and rollback point per stage.
  2. Re-check the current state immediately before every R3 effect: the remote, branch, commit, checks, and pending reviews.
  3. Stop the batch on the first failed verification, conflicting instruction, or unexpected change by someone else, and report rather than work around it.

Autonomy raises the cost of an unverified claim. The core principles on verification and evidence apply with the same force here as in any other profile.

docs.title: Profile: guided
docs.text: For people who are new to agent-assisted delivery, or experienced people working in an unfamiliar domain, repository, or production surface. The goal is a correct result and a person who understands how it was reached.

docs.title: Autonomy by action class
docs.text: Class Behavior R0 — read-only Autonomous within scope. Summarize what was inspected and what it means. R1 — reversible local write Propose a short plan first: files to change, why, and how to undo it. Act after the person confirms. A single obvious edit in a file the person named may proceed and be explained afterwards. R2 — destructive Explicit, target-specific approval immediately before the action, after explaining the consequence and the recovery path in plain language. R3 — external effect Explicit approval for each effect (push, pull request, merge, deployment, message), after showing exactly what will be sent and where.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
1. Restate the goal and acceptance criteria before starting, and ask when they are missing.
  2. Explain the reason behind each significant step, naming the core principle it applies when that helps, such as "inspecting before mutating".
  3. Avoid unexplained jargon. Define a term the first time it appears.
  4. Show commands before running them when they change state.
  5. End with a short checklist: what was done, how it was verified, what the person should check, and what remains.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
1. Prefer small increments. One objective per change and no batch delivery.
  2. Validate each increment before starting the next, including the path a real user follows.
  3. When a mistake happens, explain what went wrong, how it was detected, and how to prevent it. This is the moment the profile is meant to teach.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text: When the work is coursework, apply the academic overlay as well: ask about the course's AI policy and the student's preferred mode (hints, review, or write and explain) before writing anything.

docs.title: Moving on
docs.text: When the person routinely anticipates the plan and the checks, the standard profile is likely a better fit.

docs.title: Profile: standard
docs.text: For practitioners who are comfortable reviewing agent work and want the agent to proceed within an authorized scope. This is the default profile.

docs.title: Autonomy by action class
docs.text: Class Behavior R0 — read-only Autonomous within scope. R1 — reversible local write Autonomous when the task authorizes local changes and the rollback path is clear. Ask when the target is ambiguous or the scope would expand. R2 — destructive Explicit, target-specific approval immediately before the action. R3 — external effect Explicit approval for the effect. The person may authorize a set of effects for the current task, such as "push the branch and open the pull request"; that authorization does not extend to merge, deployment, or other tasks.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
1. Confirm the goal only when it is ambiguous; otherwise state assumptions briefly and proceed.
  2. Report at meaningful points: a decision made, a blocker found, the work completed.
  3. Close with the result, the validation performed, any durable commit or pull request, and what remains unverified.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text: Follow the default operating flow and the delivery defaults. Batch delivery only when requested, with a validation and rollback point per stage.

docs.title: A-Dev learning loop
docs.text:
Daily work is A-Dev's raw material. This loop turns it into evidence, then into candidate patterns, then, when the evidence justifies it, into A-Dev practices, overlays, defaults, or core principles. It follows the pattern lifecycle.

task closed -> lessons? -> evidence in overlay -> candidate pattern -> proposal to A-Dev -> adopted layer

docs.title: When to run
docs.text:
• Before your final message in any turn where you changed files, fixed a mistake, or learned something non-obvious, even when the message ends with a question for the user. Waiting for the task to be formally closed means the loop rarely runs.
  • At the close of a task that involved a decision, a failure, a surprise, a workaround, or a non-obvious verification.
  • Immediately after an incident, a failed check, a rollback, or a correction by the user.
  • When the user asks to record, capture, or learn from the work.

Skip it for routine work that produced nothing new; say so in one line rather than inventing a lesson.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Harvest. List what this task taught, in one sentence each: what failed or surprised, what fixed it, what would have prevented it, and what the user corrected. Keep only items that would change how a future task is done.
  2. Locate the overlay. Use the personal overlay registered in the agent's guidance (the line Overlay <name> written by the A-Dev installer). If none is registered, report the lessons in the final message and suggest creating one from the template.
  3. Record evidence. Follow the overlay's own SKILL.md. Search its evidence/INDEX.md first and update an existing record when the subject matches; otherwise create a dated record from its templates (adev capture <daily|incident|session> --title "..." scaffolds one), then commit it locally in the overlay. Facts only: what happened, what was tried, the result, the verification, what remains. Sanitize: no secrets, raw sensitive output, names, customers, or internal hosts.
  4. Update candidate patterns. For each transferable lesson, add evidence to an existing candidate in the overlay's patterns/ or add a new candidate with context, an observable statement, and links to the evidence. Record counter-evidence too.
  5. Check promotion. A candidate is ready to propose when it meets the adoption criteria: observed more than once or costly once, would have changed the outcome, the narrowest A-Dev layer is clear, it is observable, and it can be stated without private context.
  6. Propose to A-Dev. For a ready candidate, prepare a sanitized change to A-Dev: a public candidate in patterns/, or an edit to the narrowest layer (overlay, practice, default; the core only for rules that hold everywhere). Opening a pull request is an external effect: do it only when the user or a durable grant authorizes it; otherwise leave the branch or the drafted text and say so.
  7. Report. In the final message, list what was recorded, which candidates changed, and what was proposed or is ready to propose.

docs.title: Authority
docs.text: Registering an overlay with the A-Dev installer authorizes this loop, in every profile, to write sanitized records in that overlay and commit them locally there. Do this without asking, even in the guided profile, and mention it in the final message. Pushing the overlay, writing anywhere else, and opening pull requests to A-Dev remain external effects that need the user's explicit authorization.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
• Loading this skill does not authorize pushes or pull requests.
  • Never fabricate a lesson, a metric, or a recurrence. One observation is a candidate, not a rule.
  • Keep private evidence private. What reaches A-Dev is the sanitized pattern and a summary of the evidence.
  • Prefer making an existing rule more precise over adding a new one.

docs.title: Starter Kit
docs.text:
The A-Dev starter kit is the shortest path from doctrine to repeatable practice across repos, teams, and industries.

This is the implementation kit for the A-Dev practice. For agent capability design, also use the Hardness skill contract.

docs.title: Adoption path
docs.text:
• DAY_0.md: establish the minimum operating skeleton.
  • FIRST_WEEK.md: run the first evidence-backed iteration cycle.
  • FIRST_RELEASE.md: close the first release with traceability and verification.
  • OPERATING_RITUALS.md: compact rituals derived from the execution history of Homedir, the project where A-Dev was first proven.
  • examples/minimal-adev-loop/: a minimal, repo-agnostic sample to model the workflow.
  • personal-overlay/: a private layer for one person's working model, evidence, and candidate patterns.

docs.title: Existing assets
docs.text:
• BASELINE_template.json: machine-readable baseline seed.
  • DECISION_LOG.md: capture decisions and reversals.
  • QUALITY_CYCLE_checklist.md: broad quality cycle checklist.

docs.title: Use rule
docs.text: Do not treat these files as theory-only templates. Copy, adapt, and keep them aligned with the actual repository you are operating.

docs.title: Day 0
docs.text: Goal: establish the minimum A-Dev operating skeleton before prompting for meaningful implementation.

docs.title: Required outputs
docs.text:
1. A baseline source of truth.
  2. A visible roadmap or initiative list.
  3. A decision log.
  4. A place to store prompts or iteration requests.
  5. A short definition of done for the first change.

docs.title: Day 0 checklist
docs.text:
• Copy or adapt BASELINE_template.json into the target repo's canonical baseline format.
  • Create ROADMAP.md or equivalent.
  • Create a decision log seeded with project constraints and known red lines.
  • Define one small change with a short feedback path and a clear rollback boundary.
  • State the validation path before implementation begins.

docs.title: Red lines
docs.text:
• Do not start with a large refactor.
  • Do not invent workflows the repo does not support.
  • Do not let the first iteration depend on production-only secrets or heavy external setup.

docs.title: Exit criteria
docs.text: By the end of day 0, a new repo should know: - what rules govern work, - what problem is next, - how success will be validated, - where the resulting evidence will be stored.

docs.title: Decision Log
docs.text: Use one entry per decision. Keep it short and link to evidence.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
• Date:
  • Decision:
  • Options considered:
  • Rationale (persona + baseline/constraint):
  • Evidence (commit/CI/flag link):
  • Follow-up guardrail/baseline update:

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-01-11
  • Decision: Keep EvenFlow UI server-rendered; no heavy SPA framework.
  • Options: SPA with complex JS vs SSR with simple components.
  • Rationale: Frugality + consistency; avoid bloat and speed up verification.
  • Evidence: Commit XYZ with SSR templates + health checks green; flag controls applied.
  • Follow-up: Added “SSR-first, no heavy middleware” to baseline.

docs.title: First Release
docs.text: Goal: move from internal iteration to a release candidate without losing traceability.

docs.title: Release checklist
docs.text:
• Confirm the scope is still atomic and understandable.
  • Re-run the focused validation path for the release surface.
  • Verify baseline, roadmap, and decision log do not contradict the implementation.
  • Summarize what changed, why it matters, and what remains out of scope.
  • Define rollback or recovery expectations when relevant.

docs.title: Evidence package
docs.text: A first release should leave behind: - branch and PR traceability, - validation notes, - updated baseline or guardrails when new failure modes appeared, - a short release summary that a future agent can follow.

docs.title: Release discipline
docs.text:
• Do not promote a release that cannot be explained in one paragraph.
  • Do not hide risk behind broad wording.
  • Do not tag or publish solely because work exists; release when the scope is coherent and validated.

docs.title: First Week
docs.text: Goal: complete a small but fully evidenced delivery loop and learn from it.

docs.title: Week 1 objectives
docs.text:
• Run at least one atomic iteration from definition to evidence.
  • Capture at least one decision in the log.
  • Update the baseline with one concrete lesson.
  • Close one walkthrough or smoke-test-backed change.

docs.title: Suggested sequence
docs.text:
1. Pick one change with narrow blast radius.
  2. Define the expected validation before implementation.
  3. Implement in a dedicated branch.
  4. Run focused validation.
  5. Record evidence: commit, check result, walkthrough note, or smoke test.
  6. Translate any failure into a reusable rule.

docs.title: What good looks like
docs.text:
• The team can point to one finished loop, not just partial code.
  • Prompt quality improved because the baseline was updated.
  • The repo now contains a stronger operating rule than it had at the start of the week.

docs.title: Avoid
docs.text:
• Chasing many half-finished improvements.
  • Treating a green build as the only evidence.
  • Leaving important lessons trapped in chat or memory.

docs.title: Operating Rituals
docs.text: These rituals convert A-Dev from aspiration into repeatable behavior.

docs.title: 1. Pre-iteration ritual
docs.text:
• State scope in one paragraph.
  • State the validation path before implementation.
  • Confirm the baseline still matches repo reality.

docs.title: 2. Failure-to-rule ritual
docs.text:
• When something breaks, stop adding scope.
  • Identify whether the failure came from definition, implementation, validation, or environment.
  • Write the smallest reusable rule that would have prevented repetition.

docs.title: 3. Multilingual sweep ritual
docs.text:
• Review touched UI surfaces for hardcoded text.
  • Check edge views, admin surfaces, and recently added flows.
  • Treat language drift as product debt, not a cosmetic follow-up.

docs.title: 4. CI/CD recovery ritual
docs.text:
• Confirm the build path, image path, and deployment path tell the same story.
  • Validate user-visible behavior, not only process liveness.
  • Update documentation if the real delivery path differs from the written one.

docs.title: 5. Performance ritual
docs.text:
• Compare against a concrete baseline.
  • Measure error rate and latency before proposing redesign.
  • Rank fixes by measured leverage.

docs.title: 6. Backup/DR ritual
docs.text:
• Validate restore viability, not only backup generation.
  • Treat retention and rotation as part of reliability.
  • Preserve the recovery procedure as a reusable asset.

docs.title: 50/50 Broad Quality Cycle Checklist
docs.text:
Treat creation and verification as one continuous movement. The 50/50 principle is a symbol of balanced attention, not an exact time split or universal iteration length.

  • [ ] Definition written (scope in/out, persona, success behavior)
  • [ ] Baseline guardrails linked (security, frugality, UI consistency)
  • [ ] Prompt ready with context + constraints + quality gates
  • [ ] Progressive-delivery control defined when the change needs one
  • [ ] Focused build, analysis, and tests executed for the affected surface
  • [ ] User or system walkthrough completed in the relevant configuration
  • [ ] Evidence captured (commit/CI links, decision log entry)
  • [ ] Baseline updated if anything failed or changed
  • [ ] Rollback or containment path verified when relevant

docs.title: Minimal A-Dev Loop Example
docs.text: This example is intentionally small. It shows the minimum structure needed to run A-Dev in a new repository without depending on a specific tool, model, or Homedir-specific context.

docs.title: Included files
docs.text:
• BASELINE.md: operating rules.
  • ROADMAP.md: current next move.
  • prompts/iteration-01.md: first scoped request.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Copy the structure into a target repo.
  2. Replace the placeholders with real constraints.
  3. Run one atomic change and capture the resulting evidence.
  4. Update the baseline with one lesson before starting the next iteration.

docs.title: BASELINE
docs.text:
• Keep scope atomic.
  • Validate before and after implementation.
  • Record evidence for every completed iteration.
  • Turn repeated failure into a reusable rule.
  • Prefer simple, explainable changes over broad redesign.

docs.title: Current iteration
docs.text: Ship one small change that can be defined, implemented, validated, and explained in a single session.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• No broad refactor.
  • No undocumented workflow assumptions.
  • Validation path must be known before implementation starts.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Implement one small, reversible improvement with a known validation path.

docs.title: Required evidence
docs.text:
• commit or patch summary,
  • validation result,
  • one lesson added back into the baseline.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• unrelated cleanup,
  • speculative redesign,
  • undocumented shortcuts.

docs.title: Personal overlay template
docs.text:
A personal overlay is your private layer on top of A-Dev: how you like to work, the evidence of what you and your agents actually did, and the lessons that might one day become shared doctrine. A-Dev stays public and generic; the overlay stays yours.

A-Dev (public)           core doctrine, Hardness, profiles, overlays, practices
  └─ your overlay        working model, evidence, candidate patterns  (private)
       └─ repository     the project's own AGENTS.md and checks

docs.title: Create yours
docs.text:
1. Copy this directory into a new private repository.
  2. Rename the skill: change name: in SKILL.md to a unique lowercase name, such as jdoe-context, and adjust its description.
  3. Fill in profile/working-model.md. Keep it short; agents read it at the start of every session.
  4. Install it together with A-Dev:
bash install/bootstrap.sh --workspace "$HOME/workspace" --profile standard \
  --overlay-repo https://github.com/<you>/<your-overlay>.git

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
Path Purpose Loaded SKILL.md Session startup and evidence maintenance for agents Every session profile/working-model.md Language, delegation style, verification expectations, environment, profile Every session evidence/INDEX.md One line per evidence record, newest first Every session evidence/daily/, evidence/incidents/, evidence/sessions/ Dated, sanitized records On demand templates/ Shapes for daily, incident, and session records When writing patterns/ Candidate patterns and their promotion to A-Dev On demand

Agents load only the working model and the index at startup. The context stays small as evidence grows, and agents open a record when a task needs it.

docs.title: Rules that still apply
docs.text: The overlay specializes A-Dev; it cannot weaken it. In particular, data protection applies in private repositories too: no secrets, raw sensitive output, customer details, or internal URLs. Use neutral roles such as "the operator" and "the customer environment".

docs.title: Agent instructions
docs.text:
This repository is a private A-Dev personal overlay. Follow SKILL.md for session startup and evidence maintenance, and A-Dev for delivery.

  • Keep records sanitized and impersonal, even though the repository is private.
  • One subject per record; link related records instead of repeating them.
  • Keep profile/working-model.md short. Move detail into evidence records and link to them.
  • Reusable doctrine belongs in A-Dev, not here. Record candidate patterns in patterns/ and promote them through a pull request to A-Dev.

docs.title: Personal overlay
docs.text: This overlay specializes A-Dev for one person. It never weakens A-Dev's core doctrine or the user's explicit instructions in the current session.

docs.title: Session startup
docs.text:
Read, from this skill's directory, before other task work:

  1. profile/working-model.md.
  2. evidence/INDEX.md.

Do not read every evidence record at startup. Open a record from the index when the task needs it. Resolve paths from this skill's repository directory, including when installed through a filesystem link. If a required file is missing, report it instead of inventing the owner's preferences.

Historical records are dated observations. They do not prove the current state of any system, the completion of pending actions, or a universal recommendation.

docs.title: Maintain evidence
docs.text:
Record evidence when the A-Dev learning loop runs (at the close of a meaningful task, and after a failure or correction) or when the owner asks. Registering this overlay authorizes those local writes and local commits; it never authorizes a push or any other remote write.

  1. Search the index and related records first. Update the best existing record; create a dated record only for a distinct subject.
  2. Use the matching template in templates/. Record what happened, what was tried, the result, the verification, and what remains. Never fabricate commands, outputs, timings, metrics, or resolutions.
  3. Attribute AI assistance: the tool, the exact model only when known, its contribution, the human role, and the corrections needed.
  4. Sanitize before saving: no secrets, sensitive raw output, personal identifiers, customer details, internal URLs, or private environment names.
  5. Add or update the record's line in evidence/INDEX.md.
  6. Commit the record locally in this repository (evidence: <title>), including only the files you wrote. Never push unless the owner asks.
  7. When a lesson looks transferable, add it to patterns/ as a candidate with links to its evidence. Promotion to A-Dev happens through a pull request to A-Dev, within the owner's authorized scope.

docs.text:

docs.title: Candidate patterns
docs.text: A candidate pattern is a lesson that might transfer beyond the situation where it was observed. It stays here until the evidence justifies promoting it to A-Dev.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
### Short imperative name

**Status:** candidate | proposed to A-Dev (link) | promoted (link) | retired
**Context:** when it applies, and when it does not.
**Pattern:** what to do, stated so that compliance can be observed.
**Evidence:** links to the records where it was observed, with dates. Note counter-evidence too.

docs.title: Promotion
docs.text:
Propose a pattern to A-Dev when:

  1. It was observed more than once, or a single failure was costly enough to justify it.
  2. It would have changed the outcome in the cases recorded.
  3. The narrowest A-Dev layer is clear: an overlay, a practice, a default, or, rarely, the core.
  4. It can be stated without private context, names, or environment details.

Open a pull request to A-Dev with the sanitized pattern and a summary of the evidence. The detailed records stay here. Follow the A-Dev pattern promotion process.
